“Script Tag src Attribute Behavior When Internal Content Exists”

The presence of both external source loading via src and inline script content introduces ambiguity because browser implementations and specific tools, like Google’s indexers, might interpret this structure differently.

Behavior Regarding Script Execution

Different environments exhibit varying levels of adherence to web standards, leading to inconsistent execution models when both src and inline content are present:

  • Strict/Modern Browsers: Some browsers execute the script referenced by src first, potentially ignoring the internal content afterward, or they might only execute based on the src if present.
  • Lenient Browsers: Other agents might attempt to load the external resource specified by src. Even if the loading process fails or succeeds, they proceed to evaluate the inline content. This unreliable behavior violates modern HTML5 constraints and should be avoided for robust development.

item.title: Resolve JavaScript 'clear' Function Shadowing with HTML Inline Events
item.description:
“Resolve JavaScript ‘clear’ Function Shadowing with HTML Inline Events”

Encountering issues where your custom JavaScript function, specifically named clear, fails to execute when triggered by an HTML inline event attribute like onclick? This is a common point of confusion in web development, primarily stemming from how browsers create scopes for inline event handlers.

When you define an event handler directly within an HTML attribute (e.g., <button onclick="clear()">), the browser creates a specific execution scope for that inline script. This scope, as detailed in the HTML Standard , includes several objects that can lead to naming conflicts. Crucially, document is added to this scope. This means properties and methods of the document object can be accessed directly by their names.

item.title: Safely Include External Scripts in HTML: Overcoming </script> Tag Conflicts
item.description:
“Safely Include External Scripts in HTML: Overcoming Tag Conflicts”

When embedding external JavaScript files within an HTML document, a common challenge arises: the HTML parser can mistakenly interpret the closing </script> tag within your JavaScript code as the termination of the entire <script> block. This can lead to unexpected behavior and script execution errors. This occurs because, according to SGML standards, the sequence </ signifies an end-tag open delimiter (ETAGO). While modern browsers generally handle CDATA script blocks by looking for an actual </script> tag, older parsing methods or stricter XHTML interpretations can cause issues.

This is why direct element.click() calls may not always work as expected, especially in browsers like Firefox and Opera in certain contexts.

item.title: What is javascript:void(0) in HTML Links?
item.description:
“What is javascript:void(0) in HTML Links?”

The use of javascript:void(0) within the href attribute of an HTML anchor (<a>) tag is a common practice, but its purpose and implications are often debated. Let’s delve into what it means and why developers choose this approach, along with exploring alternative methods.

The void operator in JavaScript evaluates an expression and subsequently returns the primitive value undefined. When used in the context of a link’s href, like javascript:void(0), it essentially tells the browser to execute a JavaScript snippet that returns undefined.

Solution 1: Explicitly Set Button Type
